```{r}
# Path of folder where we are storing our results
absolute_path <- "~/Documents/uni/Theoretical Eco&Evo/Code/"
```
Why did we do the step above?



```{r}
# Part 1: Simple function to multiply integers from 1 to 20 by parameter value ("multiplier")
get.multiples1to10 <- function(multiplier) {
  numbers <- 1:10
  return(multiplier * numbers)
}

# Part 2: Display results for parameter value set to 3
current_value <- 3
results <- get.multiples1to10(multiplier = current_value)
print(results) 

# Part 3: Storing our file
the_filename <- paste(absolute_path, "multiples1to10--multiplier", current_value, ".csv")
print(the_filename)
write.csv(results, file = the_filename, row.names = FALSE)

```
# Legend
The code above does the following: 
Part 1: creates the function and gives it a name. function(multiplier) declares that it takes one input, multiplier, which acts as a placeholder for whatever number you pass in. The { opens the function body, where the code to run is written. When you call get.multiples1to10(3), multiplier is 3 inside the function. 1:10 means “from 1 to 10 in steps of 1”). The vector is stored in a variable called "numbers". multiplier * numbers multiplies every element of the vector by multiplier. R does this for all 10 elements at once (vectorization), so no loop is needed. return(...) then sends that result back to the caller. For multiplier = 3, it returns 3 6 9 12 15 18 21 24 27 30. The closing } after it ends the function body.

You can even if you're searching for lets say a variable that called "e" and want to replace it with "elephant" you can go on "find", search "e" and click on "whole word" so it doesn't also change every word that has an "e" in it.
